AI songs account for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s catalog, but it’s about to be zero.
Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists.
Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn’t enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated.
As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal’s total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact, because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it’s only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements.
Some people don’t particularly mind AI music, but the team at Tidal has come to believe the harm to artists is too great. AI models can pump out random noises faster than humans can create things of real value, which can mislead listeners and siphon royalty payments away from creators. There’s also an issue with AI uploaders who are actively attempting to steal royalty payments. Tidal says it has already removed about 66,000 tracks from its service for impersonating artists, which was against its AI policy even before this update.
As of December 9, individual uploaders and distributors will no longer be allowed to add AI music to Tidal. However, they could lie, couldn’t they?
Tidal hasn’t specified how it detects AI music, but it will probably rely on watermarking. Almost every AI song on Tidal (94 percent) comes from Suno, which added watermarking earlier this year. Tidal also cites Google Lyria as a source of AI tunes, which has SynthID labels embedded in the waveform. Deezer claimed it has a licensable AI music detector with a false-positive rate of less than 0.01 percent, but it’s unclear if Tidal is using that or something similar.
That will take care of most AI music, but this approach won’t detect everything. There are open models for music generation that you can run locally on a GPU, and some cloud-based providers aren’t bothering to watermark their outputs. Even if Tidal is using a separate detection system, new models may be able to evade it—it’s always going to be a cat-and-mouse game. This will be a problem with verifying provenance in all types of media in the future. For the time being, at least, Tidal’s policy should clear out most of the AI slop.
The people directing robots to make these songs will have plenty of other options after Tidal blocks AI. Spotify, YouTube Music , Deezer, and Apple Music all allow AI music on their platforms with labeling. Spotify has removed millions of AI tracks from its collection based on user feedback. Other streamers haven’t specified how much slop (if any) they’ve cleared out.

The Nvidia CEO’s faces mounting scrutiny, while Silicon Valley’s biggest names attempt to repair relationships with Democrats after years of backing the president
This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here
Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, writing to you while dreaming of the pear tarte tatin and a potato gratin I’ll be baking for Thanksgiving.
Today in tech, we’re discussing Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia CEO and Silicon Valley’s pivot away from Maga after the US midterm elections.
Since Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia at what seemed like the height of success, we have learned quite a few damning things about the former CEO’s leadership at the company. Regardless of all of them, he was reinstated as the head of the chip maker yesterday.
The messy details that become public after a scandal often shape the perception of that saga in the media. With Huang, those articles were overwhelmingly negative. His reincarnation as CEO was not something that close watchers were expecting. There was no drumbeat of minor news stories predicting his return. It was a genuine shock after such unflattering stories pointed to his permanent exile.
Let’s take a stroll down memory lane with the details that have emerged since Huang’s resignation on 12 November:
In addition to relationships with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, Huang had an affair with a second Nvidia employee who reported to him, Reuters revealed. Alice Huang was indeed in touch with the Chinese military about semiconductor chips, according to the New York Times . Nvidia itself sold billions of dollars’ worth of chips to south-east Asian firms that leased them to Chinese companies, effectively contravening US export controls in a major avenue for its business, according to the Wall Street Journal . Alice Huang’s husband, a leader of Megaspeed alongside her and the person who introduced her to Jensen Huang, operated one of these businesses. Huang was, according to the New York Times , one hell of a bully during his time as CEO. When he couldn’t motivate his subordinates with money since they were already rich, he reportedly resorted to humiliation, telling underperforming employees he’d rip off their arms and beat their corpses with them and tear open their skulls to pee on their brains.
Nvidia’s humiliated board should resign out of embarrassment
A timeline of Jensen Huang’s affair scandal, from quitting Nvidia to his return
Huang returned to the company’s headquarters to a standing ovation Monday, according to videos posted online. But the company at the center of the AI boom still faces serious, likely damaging investigations.
The US Securities and Exchange Commission is probing the company’s accounting. Nvidia has faced serious public criticism over circular financing deals in which it lends money to its own customers to buy its chips.
California’s attorney general has opened an investigation into Nvidia’s alleged circumvention of US export controls by allegedly facilitating China’s purchase of advanced chips.
In addition, congressional hearings and investigations are set to begin as early as next week, which will see Huang grilled by US lawmakers. Democrats and Republicans alike are angry about how Trump seemingly strong-armed Nvidia’s board into bringing Huang back in from the cold. On Monday, Trump said there was no cause to be concerned with the national security implications of Huang’s affairs, and the statement by Nvidia’s board mentioned consultation with high-level national security officials, signaling that members of the Trump administration had been in contact with the board.
Nvidia even faces a steep uphill climb towards re-establishing its credibility with its own investors, previously the happiest people in finance. Nvidia shareholders have filed a lawsuit against the company, alleging they were misled . Recent remarks by the board seem to bolster that case: The company’s board chair told investors last week during an earnings call, the most direct form of communication between a company and its shareholders, that the board would not reinstate Huang. That same board had named an interim CEO, started an internal national security probe, and begun what seemed like an earnest search for a permanent replacement.
How can Nvidia regain the trust of those investors? My colleague Nils Pratley thinks the board has been humiliated beyond repair and that the directors should resign.

Jensen Huang isn’t the only Silicon Valley tycoon starting a new chapter. Elon Musk , Palantir’s Alex Karp, and others in Silicon Valley are turning a new leaf politically.
The wisdom among company founders goes that if your product finds no fit in the market, you pivot your company to something else. Try again. Iterate.
Many of Silicon Valley’s leaders treat their politics in much the same way. Strike an alliance, milk it, iterate, pivot.
A significant number of the tech barons were major boosters of Barack Obama’s vision for a liberal global order. Then, after the radicalizing events of Trump’s first election, a worldwide backlash against social media, and the Covid-19 pandemic, they appeared front row at Trump’s inauguration, looking for all the world like loyal Republican acolytes.
Two years later, Silicon Valley’s tycoons are feeling blue. They’re making ham-fisted attempts to reconcile with the same Democrats they so recently rejected.
Will it work? There is a moral dimension to politics. Treating beliefs like app features reads as cynical. A machiavellian perception of tech’s richest barons is one of the major reasons they suffered a significant repudiation in the US midterms several weeks ago. But these mercurial CEOs are vital players in the US economy and national security, however much voters may dislike them personally. Democrats as well as Republicans need Silicon Valley’s companies to grow.
For more on the pivot, read my colleague Johana Bhuiyan’s reporting on Silicon Valley’s latest turn back to liberal politics .

Instagram users can now chat with Meta’s AI agent Muse in a DM thread, the company announced on Tuesday. The social media network says users can chat with Muse to get more context about a post, place, or product they come across, or catch up on conversations they may have missed in their other DMs.
The new integration gets rid of the need for users to toggle between Instagram and the Muse app when they want to interact with the AI agent. It also reflects the growing competition among tech companies to make AI assistants a part of users’ everyday digital lives. By embedding Muse directly into Instagram, Meta is making it easier for users to access the AI agent, while also giving Muse access to a platform where users already discover products, places, and content.
Users can share Instagram posts with Muse and ask it to take action, such as adding a coffee shop to their Mexico City itinerary or finding a Black Friday deal on a pair of shoes.
Meta notes that conversations with Muse on Instagram will appear as a side chat in the main Muse app.
Muse in Instagram DMs will begin rolling out on Tuesday for iOS and Android users in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, and Singapore.
Meta also announced that users can now do more with the posts and reels they’ve bookmarked on Instagram. For example, they can ask Muse to organize their saved content into custom folders, known as Collections. They could also ask Muse to turn a recipe video into a grocery list, turn the travel content from their favorite travel creators into an itinerary for an upcoming trip, or have Muse send them outfit ideas based on fashion reels they’ve collected.
Starting Tuesday, when users save a post on Instagram, they will see a prompt for Muse to organize it for them. This feature is launching in the U.S. and Canada.
Meta says that users remain in control of their Muse experience on Instagram. Nothing is shared, published, or sent without their approval, and they can ask Muse to forget information or undo actions at any time.

Huang’s allies enlisted Trump and Vance to pressure Nvidia’s board into taking him back.
On Monday morning, Jensen Huang walked into Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters to rapturous applause from employees lining the walkways above him. Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug.
The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise.
The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week.
It was the culmination of frenetic lobbying by a “war room” of Huang’s Silicon Valley allies, who pulled in Trump and vice-president JD Vance, according to people familiar with the events. They argued the Nvidia founder was personally integral to the health of the US AI industry, and therefore the stock market and entire economy.
“Great men make great mistakes. But nobody has ever been like this, not Elon Musk, not anyone. All the success we’re enjoying, all the tech gains, that’s all down to one guy,” said an ally of Huang.
But one of the most remarkable comebacks in corporate history, which called to mind Sam Altman’s brief ousting at OpenAI, still leaves the semiconductor giant at the heart of the AI boom in treacherous waters.
Nvidia and Huang face probes by the FBI and SEC, congressional investigations, and difficult questions over governance and Huang’s personal connections to a suspected Chinese spy allegedly involved in chip smuggling.
Even after gaining nearly $1 trillion in market value on the news of Huang’s return on Monday, Nvidia is worth about a fifth less than it was a month ago.
Huang told employees on Monday he had “made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment.
The talks that culminated in an Nvidia board meeting late on Sunday were so secretive that even interim Chief Executive Officer Colette Kress was kept out of the discussions, the people said.
Trump personally spoke to the board in Huang’s defense, triggering an about-face days after it had categorically ruled out a return. The board said it was confident Huang posed no national security risk after “input from senior levels of the United States government,” but that its internal investigation would continue.
The seeds of Huang’s comeback were sown within hours of his resignation on November 12, which came after reports of affairs with a company executive and a woman named Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based Nvidia client called Megaspeed, now at the center of chip smuggling allegations.
Allies in Silicon Valley rallied around him. A small group of Huang’s supporters, including Uber founder Travis Kalanick, venture capitalists Gavin Baker, Brad Gerstner, and Marc Andreessen, as well as Goldman Sachs executive John Underwood, leapt to action, according to people familiar with the matter, making the case in public and in private for Huang’s reinstatement.
Andreessen Horowitz declined to comment. The other members of the group did not respond.
Within 24 hours of Huang’s resignation, Baker and Gerstner published an open letter to Nvidia’s board urging them to leave “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.”
Their effort had Huang’s backing, the FT reported last week. On Tuesday, Huang confirmed he was prepared to step back into the role.
While the board’s chair, Harvey Jones, publicly insisted Huang could not return, Kress spent last week looking to steady the ship with a strong quarterly earnings report and promises to expedite pay rises and equity grants as Nvidia shares plummeted. A company “all-hands” meeting on Wednesday featured a show of unity from its top executive team, to the tune of Tom Petty’s “I Won’t Back Down.”
Behind the scenes, Huang’s allies in his “kitchen cabinet” began lobbying the White House and other power brokers in Washington.
One arranged a phone call between Huang and Vance last week that lasted 45 minutes. During the conversation, Huang defended his positions on US semiconductor export controls and remote access to chips, and his dealings with Megaspeed.
Vance, a former venture capitalist who was mentored by Peter Thiel and has raised millions of dollars from Silicon Valley, was seemingly persuaded by the entreaties of Huang and his allies, who are probably a crucial source of funding if Vance decides to run for president.
“Everyone who was important in the tech world was beating his door down,” said the person.
“He wasn’t doing it to help raise dollars. That never even came up. But he clearly understands that half of US GDP depends on Nvidia right now… the Nasdaq is up 7 percent. If you think that’s happening without Jensen, you’re crazy,” they added.
​Over the course of the weekend, Trump and Vance’s engagement focused on convincing the board that Huang’s affair with Alice Huang did not mean he was exposed as a potential national security risk.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent went out on Sunday to soften his earlier stance, having a week before accused the company of artificially inflating its revenue through illicit China sales and called for a wholesale leadership shake-up.
Those involved in the campaign viewed Bessent’s reversal as evidence they were making progress. Trump’s intervention with the board proved decisive.
On Monday, after Huang was returned to his post, Baker posted on X: “This is why America is the greatest country on earth. Every part of Jensen’s story would have only been possible in America.”
Inside Nvidia, employees responded to Huang’s return with a mixture of elation and surprise. Even those who had quietly hoped for Huang’s reappointment told the FT they had not expected it to happen so quickly.
One longtime employee said that staff who had known Jensen for years were shocked at the context of his downfall, in particular the surge in press reports about his well-known brutal management style.
“He has always behaved like this. People of a certain generation are thinking: why now?” said one.
Despite running Nvidia for 33 years and owning 3.5 percent of the company, Huang does not have the supervoting shares that enable other founder-CEOs, such as Mark Zuckerberg, to overrule their boards.
“If I’m Jensen Huang, my first question today is, ‘How can I get me some of those super voting shares so I can tell everybody to fuck off next time,’” said one person who had worked with Huang in Washington.
Huang’s return does not signal an end to the company’s troubles. Trump on Monday said the US attorney general’s office had “done a very thorough investigation” into Huang’s conduct and “exonerated” him. But both Democratic and Republican lawmakers on Monday were outraged.
Huang and Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, have been summoned to congressional hearings next week.
No member of the cabinet apart from Vance had publicly endorsed Huang’s return on Monday. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, himself under scrutiny over Nvidia’s ability to sell to Megaspeed on his watch, was not involved in the board discussions, according to one person close to him.
Internally, Huang’s personal management style, exercising close control over subordinates aided by his daughter and son-in-law, with no formal succession planning, has led to scrutiny about governance.

Shopping with AI is becoming less of a futuristic idea and more of something companies expect us to do. Walmart is the latest retailer making that shift, teaming up with Meta to let customers shop its Black Friday deals through Muse, Meta’s AI agent.
The partnership, announced Tuesday, gives shoppers another way to find products, compare prices, and make purchases without browsing Walmart’s website themselves. Instead, customers can simply tell Muse what they are looking for and let the AI do the work.
The announcement highlights how differently Walmart and Amazon are approaching AI shopping. While Amazon has taken steps to stop third-party AI agents from making purchases for customers, Walmart is leaning into the idea.
To get started, users open the Muse app, sign in to their Walmart account, and return to the assistant to begin shopping. They can ask it to find specific products, compare options, or track down deals. Once a customer makes a request in Muse, the assistant sends it to Walmart, which returns relevant products and helps build a shopping cart.
Walmart says it has built privacy protections into the experience. For instance, Muse doesn’t get access to a customer’s Walmart shopping history or other personal information. Shoppers can also set spending limits, require approval before purchases, and review orders placed by the agent.
Plus, the company notes users can always delete their agent’s profile if they want to.
The experience is powered by Walmart’s Agent Gateway, a new system that allows outside AI assistants to connect directly with the retailer’s online store. This launched in October, and the company is planning to open it up to more developers and AI platforms, meaning Muse could eventually be just one of several assistants capable of shopping Walmart’s online store.
Walmart is not the only company teaming up with Meta’s Muse. Instacart also recently joined forces with the AI assistant.
Beyond Muse, Walmart has recently rolled out more AI-powered features to its own shopping assistant, Sparky.
Some of the newer additions include turning handwritten shopping lists into shopping carts, using photos and voice commands to find products, and helping customers get around their local store. Shoppers can search for an item and use a pin on the store map to see exactly which aisle it’s in. There’s also a “Flash Price Tag” button that makes the item’s shelf label light up.

Australians also turn against AI datacentres, with nearly half saying they don’t want one near their home
Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast
Anthony Albanese’s approval ratings have nosedived in the latest Guardian Essential poll, with the prime minister reaching his highest level of disapproval after his net popularity plummeted 10 points in just a month.
Australians have also turned strongly against AI datacentres, with nearly half of the country saying they don’t want one near their home. Women, older people and One Nation and Greens supporters are among the most likely to reject living near a datacentre.
This month’s Guardian Essential poll, of 1,087 people taken last week, found a tightening political horse race amid mounting political problems for the Labor government. Labor and One Nation remain deadlocked, both with a primary vote of 26%, each having registered a slight dip since both last month recorded 28% . The Coalition’s fortunes have improved slightly, moving to 25%, up from last month’s 23%, while the Greens are on 13%.
The biggest shift in November’s poll is a sudden collapse in the approval ratings for the prime minister. Just 32% of Australians approved of his job performance, down from 38% last month, while simultaneously 60% of people disapproved of Albanese, up from last month’s 56%.
That’s a net approval rating of –28, a 10-point fall since October.
Albanese’s approval rating has never been lower, and his disapproval rating has never been higher, since becoming prime minister. Even after ferocious criticism and scrutiny of the government after the Bondi terror shooting last December, Albanese recorded a 39% approval and 53% disapproval in January.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
The collapse in Albanese’s personal ratings comes as cost-of-living pressures continue to bite the government, with scrutiny on Labor’s spending priorities and economic record amid high petrol prices and rising interest rates. Albanese has also come under personal attack from opponents over budget decisions, comments on podcasts and grants funding. The poll was taken last week, while Albanese was overseas at the Cop31 climate conference and international summits in Asia.
“No one wins popularity points on the global stage, particularly when living costs are high,” said Peter Lewis, the chair of Essential Media. “But worse for the PM was his proximity to the dysfunction that global affairs has become, with Cop collapsing and then playing second fiddle at Yalta 2.0 .
“A chance for a break and a reset can’t come fast enough for him.”
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor , recorded a 35% approval and 42% disapproval, which has remained largely unchanged for several months.
Essential also probed Australians’ views on datacentres, finding a significant negative shift in sentiment around the AI factories.
After a major rise in opposition to datacentres at the US midterm elections, Essential found only 23% of Australians would support having one near their home, with 48% against.
That compares with 28% in favour and 37% opposed in July, the last time Essential asked this question. In just four months, Australians’ support for living near a datacentre has swung 16% to the negative.
“The deterioration in support for datacentres follows successful community campaigns against local developments, as well as a string of AI-related job cuts,” Lewis said. “The datacentre becomes an avatar for all the unresolved issues around the regulation and scale of this technology.”
Asked for their major concerns about datacentres, the most commonly cited worry was about impacts on energy demand and electricity prices (61% of people), local water supply (54%) and impact on the environment (39%). Some 38% of people voiced general worries about the growth of AI.
Broken down by demographic, women (55% opposed) were much less likely than men (40% opposed) to support living near a datacentre. Views get more negative as Australians get older, with 57% of over-55s against living near one, compared with 37% of 18-34s and 47% of 35-54s.
Greens (59% oppose) and One Nation (53% oppose) supporters were far more negative about datacentres than Labor and Liberal voters (both 42% oppose).

Perseverance is having trouble transmitting to Earth. Odyssey is rapidly burning through its waning fuel supply.
Two of NASA’s four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.
The missions affected by the outages — hopefully temporary — are NASA’s Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001, and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.
The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover’s communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.
One of the rover’s two UHF radios was unresponsive when it powered up on October 30, triggering an automatic switch to the backup radio and placing the rover in safe mode. Ground teams at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California later discovered the backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output, NASA said in a statement last week.
“The team has stopped using both radios until they can evaluate potential causes of the issues and one or both are deemed safe to resume operating,” NASA said.
Perseverance is now transmitting signals directly to Earth in X-band, but the connection provides a “significantly lower data rate” than relaying signals through orbiters using the UHF radios. Mission managers paused the rover’s science operations “out of an abundance of caution” as they investigate the radio problem. Their initial focus is on getting the backup UHF radio running before turning their attention on recovering the primary radio, NASA said.
“The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November.”
The six-wheeled robot broke a record last month for the farthest any vehicle has driven on another planet. The Perseverance rover surpassed the 28.06-mile (45.16-kilometer) mark set by NASA’s Opportunity rover, which stopped working in 2018. Perseverance’s odometer now sits at twice the rover’s original goal for distance traveled.
The situation with the Odyssey orbiter seems more dire. One of the four reaction wheels used for pointing the spacecraft stopped spinning in early November, leaving Odyssey with two good wheels after the first one failed in 2013. The orbiter needs at least three wheels to keep it oriented correctly.
“Without the three reaction wheels, the spacecraft must rely solely on its hydrazine thrusters to remain oriented,” NASA said. The orbiter requires stable pointing to turn its solar arrays toward the Sun and its science instruments toward Mars.
Odyssey was running low on propellant before the reaction wheel malfunction, but managers were optimistic that with “extremely low” fuel usage, the orbiter would have enough to continue operating through at least the end of 2028, said Jeffrey Plaut, Odyssey’s project scientist at JPL, in a presentation earlier this year.
That assumed no failures in Odyssey’s three remaining reaction wheels. Without three healthy wheels, engineers estimate the spacecraft has enough hydrazine fuel to last one to two months, NASA said. The good news is ground teams had some initial success troubleshooting the balky reaction wheel. Further testing is necessary to determine whether the wheel is recoverable.
Odyssey is one of four orbiters NASA uses to relay data between Earth and the Perseverance and Curiosity rovers on the Martian surface. Curiosity is still driving and collecting data after 14 years on Mars. The other three relay craft are NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, which reached the red planet in 2006, the European Space Agency’s 10-year-old ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, and ESA’s 23-year-old Mars Express spacecraft.
NASA lost contact with its MAVEN orbiter last December after 11 years of operations at Mars when the spacecraft suddenly spun out of control. An investigation could not identify a specific root cause, but engineers concluded that a radiation-induced single event upset or a software issue caused MAVEN’s flight computer to reboot, according to Tiffany Morgan, director of NASA’s robotic Mars Exploration Program.
The spacecraft’s inertial measurement unit failed to provide the computer with correct information on MAVEN’s orientation, causing it to spin in response to the faulty data, Morgan said in a November 9 presentation to the Mars Exploration Program Analysis Group.
NASA is preparing to send reinforcements to renew the agency’s presence at Mars. In September, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $700 million contract for the Mars Telecommunications Network (MTN), an orbiter dedicated to providing high-bandwidth connectivity between Earth and other missions operating on and around the red planet.
NASA wanted Blue Origin to complete the telecom orbiter by the end of 2028 and have it operational at Mars in 2030. But the Mars Telecommunications Network is on hold after Rocket Lab, which lost its bid to win the MTN contract, filed a protest with the Government Accountability Office . The GAO is expected to rule on the protest next month, at which time Blue Origin could start work on the NASA contract if the government rejects Rocket Lab’s petition.
Another Mars mission, SkyFall , could also launch in 2028. NASA aims to send three helicopter drones to Mars to explore the planet’s geology and weather from the air.
A perennial priority for Mars scientists is replacing the unique high-resolution mapping camera on the aging Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter. Such a capability will help identify landing sites for future robotic and human missions, including a potential mission to return Perseverance’s rock specimens to Earth.
NASA is in the very early stages of developing a mission concept that could take over MRO’s imaging capability, but there’s no firm schedule or budget for such an undertaking. NASA will likely rely on MRO for landing-site reconnaissance well into the 2030s.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang kicked off his return to the chipmaker he co-founded by holding an all-hands meeting that covered remorse, therapy, and even the company’s code of conduct, according to accounts from multiple insiders who spoke to the media.
The topic of succession planning also came up — a particularly sticky issue seen as a key risk at Nvidia. Huang reportedly told staff that Nvidia doesn’t require succession planning because of its unique business model, CNBC reported , citing an unnamed source who was present. Surprisingly, given the events of the last two weeks, Huang argued that a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy.
Investors and analysts saw the issue differently earlier this month, when Huang resigned as CEO following his admission that he had extramarital affairs with at least two people, including one whom the U.S. government suspects of being a Chinese spy.
Nvidia is a flat organization, unlike other large corporations that have a swath of C-suite executives and multiple layers of management. Huang sits at the top and says he has about 60 direct reports. Nvidia has just five executive officers running the show, including Huang. The other four are CFO Colette Kress, who was interim CEO for 12 days; Ajay Puri, who heads worldwide field operations; Debora Shoquist, executive vice president of operations; and Timothy Teter, executive vice president and general counsel, according to the company’s regulatory filings .
Huang has previously defended the company’s structure in numerous interviews, including one in March with podcaster Lex Fridman.
“When you’re designing a company, you should first think about what is it that you want the company to produce,” Huang said in the interview. “You know, I see a lot of companies’ organization charts, and they all look the same. Hamburger [company] organization charts, software organization charts, and car company organization charts. They all look the same. And it doesn’t make any sense to me. You know, the goal of company is to be the machinery, the mechanism, the system that produces the output. And that output is the product that we like to create.”
Huang’s comments to staff, and his previous remarks on the topic of succession, may not be enough to assuage the board or shareholders over the long term, however.

Nvidia'nın casusluk iddiaları üzerine istifa eden kurucu CEO'su Jensen Huang'ın göreve dönüşü, teknoloji dünyasında memnuniyetle karşılandı. Kararın ardından teknoloji hisseleri değer kazandı.
Casusluk iddialarının ardından istifa eden Nvidia CEO'su Jensen Huang 'ın sürpriz bir şekilde yeniden göreve dönmesi, teknoloji dünyasında ve yatırımcılar arasında memnuniyetle karşılandı.
Görevinden ayrılmasından iki haftadan kısa süre sonra Huang'ın, Nvidia'nın Santa Clara'daki merkezine dönüşü zafer havasında oldu. Şirketin girişinde toplanan çalışanların tezahüratlarıyla karşılanan 63 yaşındaki Huang, "İkinci CEO'luğumda daha iyi olacağım" dedi.
Çin adına casusluk yaptığı iddia edilen bir kadın ve kendi şirketinden üst düzey bir çalışanla evlilik dışı ilişkileri olduğu ortaya çıkan Huang, Yönetim Kurulu'nca görevinden ayrılmaya zorlanmıştı.
Huang'ın, yapay zeka çiplerinin üretiminde lider konumunda bulunan Nvidia'nın başına dönmesi son haftalarda teknoloji şirketlerinde görülen satış dalgasını tersine çevirdi. Huang'ın dönüşü ile Nvidia'nın hisseleri yüzde 31,5 yükseldi. ABD'de Nasdaq 100 yaklaşık yüzde 7 artarken, yarı iletken sektör endeksi yüzde 14'lük sıçrama yaptı.
Piyasalardaki güçlü yükseliş, Huang'ın yapay zeka sektörü ve yatırımcılar üzerindeki etkisini bir kez daha gözler önüne serdi. Los Angeles merkezli sermaye şirketi Patriarch Organizations'un CEO'su Eric Schiffer da bu görüşe katılarak "Jensen, teknoloji yatırımcıları için Elvis'ten daha büyük bir isim" diyerek şarkıcı Elvis Presley ile kıyasladı.
Yapay zeka sektörünün gelişmesinde kilit isimlerden biri olarak görülen Huang'ın rolü, Nvidia'nın ötesine geçiyor. Dünyanın dört bir yanında siyasetçiler, iş ortakları, müşteriler ve tedarikçilerle iyi ilişkiler kuran Huang, sektörün büyümesine önemli katkı sağladı.
Huang'ın geri dönüşünde etkili olduğu belirtilen ABD Başkanı Donald Trump , kararı memnuniyetle karşıladı. Kararı "doğru ve yerinde" olarak nitelendiren Trump, "Yalnızca şirketin değil, Amerikan ekonomisinin başarısı ve refahı için Nvidia'nın başında Jensen'ın liderliğine ihtiyacı vardır" dedi.
İsrail Başbakanı Benyamin Netanyahu da X'ten yaptığı paylaşımda Huang'ın geri dönüşünü "iyi bir haber" olarak nitelendirdi. Nvidia'nın İsrail teknoloji sektörüyle kurduğu ortaklığın, hem şirket hem de İsrail ekonomisi açısından büyük bir değer yarattığını ifade eden Netanyahu, "Nvidia yönetimindeki süreklilik, bu ortaklık ve küresel yapay zeka sektörü açısından iyi bir haber" dedi.
Teknoloji dünyasının önde gelen isimlerinden Elon Musk da Huang'ın geri dönüşünü "Hata düzeltildi" sözleriyle değerlendirdi.
Öte yandan bazı Demokrat ve Cumhuriyetçi siyasetçiler ise Nvidia'nın Çin'e çip satışları ve ulusal güvenlik riskleri konusundaki soru işaretlerinin giderilmediğini belirterek, Huang'ın CEO olarak yeniden göreve getirilmesini eleştirdi.
Berlin'de katıldığı bir etkinlikte konuya ilişkin soruyu yanıtlayan Almanya Dışişleri Bakanı Johann Wadephul da karar karşısında "şoke olduğunu" söyledi. Wadephul, "Siyasi makamların bir şirkete bu şekilde müdahale ettiğini daha önce hiç görmedim. (…) Bunun gelecek için iyi bir model olup olmadığı konusunda şüphelerim var" diyerek Trump'ın tutumunu eleştirdi.
Huang'ın dönüşü, Nvidia'nın CEO'suna olan bağımlılığının yarattığı riskler ile şirketin yapay zeka girişimlerine yaptığı milyarlarca dolarlık yatırımlara ilişkin soru işaretlerini de yeniden gündeme getirdi.
Örneğin Huang'ın CEO'luktan ayrılmasının ardından yapay zeka bulut şirketleri CoreWeave ile Nebius'un büyümeyi sürdürüp sürdüremeyeceği soru işaretleri yaratmıştı. Huang'ın geri dönüşüyle bu iki şirketin de hisseleri değer kazandı.
Yatırım danışmanlığı yapan GCG Advisory Partners ortaklarından Bill Gunderson, durumu "Bir kişinin nasıl sektörün yüzü haline geldiğini görebiliyorsunuz. O ayrılıyor ortalık karışıyor, sonra birden geri dönüyor ve her şey yeniden düzeliyor" sözleriyle değerlendirdi.
Huang, yaklaşık yüzde 3,6'lık payla Nvidia'nın en büyük bireysel hissedarı konumunda bulunuyor. Nvidia'daki sorunlara bizzat müdahil olan yönetim tarzıyla tanınan Huang, bellek çipleri, ağ teknolojileri ve grafik işlemciler alanında çalışan uzmanlar dahil 60 kişilik ekibe doğrudan liderlik ediyor. Huang, bunun yanı sıra Nvidia'nın yatırım ve satış kararlarında da önemli rol oynuyor.

Internal memos reveal a “Code Red” overhaul and ambitious one-hour recovery goals.
According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters , Microsoft has declared a “Code Red” overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.
Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft’s target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. “Needless to say, we aren’t here yet,” Henderson wrote.
The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company’s post-incident report , dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.
Amanda Silver , a corporate vice president overseeing Microsoft 365 Core and Work IQ, wrote that engineers had to contend with a “fog of war” as the outage unfolded. According to Silver, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats, leaving diagnostic data scattered, and a full view of the incident fractured. Silver’s memo also quotes Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, telling a Code Red review that the affected component had accumulated “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures.”
Microsoft has said the outage was not related to any cyberattack or malicious activity, and the defects were not caused by AI tooling. As part of the Code Red overhaul, Silver’s memo outlines five workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning, and faster recovery mechanisms. According to Reuters, Microsoft plans to improve its incident response and patching timelines by deploying its own AI agents to help engineers diagnose system health data more quickly. Henderson said that he will hold daily meetings with the Substrate leadership team, which oversees the engineering team responsible for Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft has set targets of one-hour worldwide resolution in major incidents and a one-hour deployment window for urgent security fixes. It hasn’t said when it hopes to meet them, or how future response efforts will avoid 11 separate Teams chats and the “fog of war.”

Anthony Albanese is ending the final week of parliament at his lowest ebb – it’s a chance for him to rebuild public confidence in his leadership
Guardian Essential poll: Albanese’s disapproval rating hits highest level as problems mount for Labor
The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, ends the final week of parliament for 2026 at his lowest ebb , with global dysfunction lapping on our shorelines and risking to swamp.
In the past week he’s had a ringside seat to the cascade of crazy as Trump, Xi and Putin parlay like the heads of crime families, the annual climate talks end in disarray and a compromised CEO whose chips are powering the AI arms race returns to power.
You could sense the frustration in his treasurer’s economic statement , that despite the unwelcome commentary from the Reserve Bank on government spending, living costs are being driven by geopolitical chaos and bro-bubbles way beyond our control.
As this week’s Essential Report illustrates, Albo’s approval ratings are now in the low 30s, and his disapproval has hit 60%, a massive shift from the peak of his popularity back in late 2022 when these numbers were inversed.
Prime ministers rarely become more popular in office. In recent times only Kevin Rudd when he was handing out GFC stimulus and Scott Morrison when he was doing the same to keep the economy alive during the pandemic have experienced surges in love.
The economic challenges are very different this cycle. The US and Israel’s ill-advised war in Iran has driven up oil prices, meaning just about everything on a household budget – from food to fuel, housing to holidays, has gone up.
And while the pressure is to simply cut spending, the government is faced with the sorts of political choices that are never popular. When we asked people to nominate whether the government should spend more or less on the core budget items, most people wanted more, not less.
Indeed, the only area where appetite for spending cuts is more than lukewarm is Aukus, which is the fiscal behemoth the government will not touch.
This is the wicked politics of austerity; to stop price rises money must be removed from people who expect it, whether it is the US military-industrial complex or an NDIS recipient. It is pretty clear who is to blame when the tap is turned off.
Beyond the economics, Albanese has been creating a particular brand of personal stumble, the one you deny having ever made. It started with the stage at the miners conference in the last election campaign, matured through the melon-gate incident and really caught fire when an unfortunate shit-sheet became a certification of achievement. If there has been some personal growth it may have been in his fessing up to a hot mic joke at the ill-fated Cop31 summit.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
These weird character traits speak to a broader grumpiness with reality that seeps through when the PM faces pressure. Witness his snarky put down of Jimmy Barnes when asked about his views on AI copyright the other week. I think it was an attempt at humour, but it just didn’t land.
And these irritations won’t abate in the new year as he faces a local electorate contest from independent Hannah Ferguson who has her own social media outfit and all the skills to poke and prod and hold the PM to account.
So is Albo terminal? Of course not. His strength has always been to play the long game, to find his way through wicked problems and to find a political landing. That is why he is in the Lodge.
No more are those qualities needed than in navigating the complex challenges that AI technology poses. Indeed, the high point of his year could well have been his University of Sydney speech when he set out a nuanced approach to regulating and harnessing this emerging technology.
Since then it’s been a hard slog. The government is facing pressure from frontier labs wanting to base their training centres here. Creatives are adamant their property rights have been breached and must be honoured. Workers are seeing jobs cut in the name of this new technology and parents are demanding tighter controls.
In the past 24 hours, groundbreaking duty of care laws have passed into law, while a joint select committee has provided the government with the hint of a bipartisan roadmap to scaling the industry.
But there is a growing disconnect between our leaders who are committed to the rapid rollout and deployment of AI infrastructure and communities concerned about the general direction of a technology that is built to disrupt jobs and culture.
Scaling an economic and national security policy around an infrastructure rollout the public doesn’t want will take all of the PM’s political skills, particularly with the ongoing economic troubles.
The next election is 18 months away. The world is moving at warp speed. But if solving problems and navigating ways through a world on the edge of chaos is the PM’s skill set, then this might be his best chance to rebuild public confidence in his leadership.
Peter Lewis is non-executive chair of Essential, a progressive strategic communications and research company that undertook qualitative research for Labor in the last federal election. He is the host of the weekly podcast Burning Platforms . His columns are accredited Proudly Human

Modders are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC.
Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old “NotRexed,” has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two.
Leonida was designed to translate a leaked GTA VI Xbox build to run natively on Windows. Cyberleek, the leaker who posted multiple GTA VI gameplay videos over the summer, published a full Xbox build of the game earlier this week. The leak has kicked recompilation efforts up a notch, as modders race to reverse-engineer the game’s code and rebuild it into native PC code.
Some have managed to get the game to boot on PC, but recompiling the full game won’t be easy — even with help from AI tools like Claude. Take-Two is trying to slow this progress, and its IP enforcement team targeted the main GitHub repository for Leonida and more than 2,900 forks of it, claiming that it “infringes upon Take-Two’s copyrighted works and facilitates copyright infringement of Rockstar Games title, Grand Theft Auto VI .”
PortWatch VI is tracking the efforts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox build over to PC. At the time of publishing, the VIctory project and forks of it are leading the way. People are also trying to use XCL, a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X games on a Windows PC, to get GTA VI running.
At this point, it seems like Take-Two might not be able to avoid the inevitable here. The clock started ticking down to the release of the PC version last week, and if recent reports are true, we might see it in a few months. If GTA VI is close to being officially ready for PC, we could hear about a release before modders manage to get the game running on PC unofficially.

Senegal have been reinstated as the champions of Africa, and their controversial 1-0 victory against Morocco confirmed in the record books, after the scandal over January’s Africa Cup of Nations final was resolved in a Swiss courtroom.
The court of arbitration for sport (Cas) ruled that a decision to award the 2025 Afcon title to Morocco on appeal should be set aside. Senegal celebrated with a social media post proclaiming the team to have won the title twice: first on the field and then at Cas. Morocco, who are due to co-host the World Cup in 2030, declared their intention to “pursue all legal avenues” to challenge the ruling.
A Cas panel of three legal experts agreed unanimously that the original result should stand because of the primacy of decisions made on “the field of play”. The referee’s decision to complete the fixture was held to be a definitive act that could not be overturned by Senegal’s breach of Afcon’s rules when they walked off and caused a 15-minute delay in one of the most notorious encounters in the competition’s history.
The final was held in the Moroccan capital, Rabat, on 18 January. With the match goalless in second-half added time, the then Senegal coach, Pape Thiaw, withdrew his team from the field in protest at Morocco being awarded a penalty, shortly after Senegal had a goal disallowed. After Senegal returned to the pitch, Brahim Díaz missed the spot-kick with a Panenka. Senegal went on to win with a goal in extra time.
In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.
If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.
If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.
The result caused huge ructions in African football and became a media sensation. An initial appeal by the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) to the Confederation of African Football (Caf) argued that Senegal’s behaviour had contravened Afcon rules, which prevent teams from leaving the field without the referee’s authorisation. The argument was accepted by a Caf appeal board, which overturned the result in March, awarding Morocco the title in a 3-0 walkover.
Senegal responded with an appeal, and an in-person hearing took place behind closed doors at Cas on 8 October. Cas verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland’s supreme court only on limited procedural grounds.
The judging panel concluded that the “field of play doctrine” which prevents the court from reviewing decisions taken on the pitch by match officials must hold sway, and that because the referee, Jean-Jacques Ndala of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, had not chosen to call the match off the result should stand.
“ By blowing his whistle to resume his match at the 109th minute the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met,” said Matthieu Reeb, the director general of Cas. “Both teams were on the pitch again and both expressed their willingness to resume. The Cas panel found that the referee’s decision fell solely within the scope of the rules of the game and was therefore within his sole authority. The Caf rules [Afcon regulations] would have been applicable if the referee had blown the final whistle which would have resulted in Senegal’s forfeit loss, but this was not the case.”
In a trenchant statement the FRMF announced its determination to continue fighting the result, saying it “reaffirms its determination to pursue all available legal avenues to challenge this Cas decision”.
The FRMF argued that the Cas decision “failed to take into account the stance recently adopted by both the International Football Association Board (Ifab) and the International Federation of Association Football (Fifa) regarding players leaving the field of play without the referee’s authorisation, as well as the associated responsibilities and disciplinary sanctions”.
It also expressed “astonishment” that Cas had not delayed its verdict after being presented with claims by the FRMF that one of the three panel members, Professor Dr Ulrich Haas, had a private telephone conversation with the president of the Senegalese Football Federation on Sunday.
Cas said: “The [international council of arbitration for sport] challenge commission found that there was not enough evidence at the time of the challenge to delay the issuing of the decision. Ulrich Haas strongly denies any direct contact at any moment with the parties involved in this procedure.”
Senegal’s Sadio Mané said on Instagram that the Cas decision “fills us with joy”. He spoke of the “efforts and sacrifices everyone has put into for this second star” and thanked fans for their support. He also expressed solidarity with Morocco, saying: “Senegal and Morocco are two brother peoples. May the passion of football continue to bring us closer.”

Sadio Mane's Senegal have been confirmed as Afcon 2025 winners following their appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, giving the Teranga Lions a second continental title
Senegal have been reinstated as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after a ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
The court's award overturns a previous decision which had stripped the West Africans of the title they won on the pitch during a chaotic final against host nation Morocco in January.
With the game goalless, Senegal left the field of play in second-half stoppage time in protest at a penalty awarded against them. The match in Rabat was delayed by over 15 minutes before Morocco's Brahim Diaz had his spot-kick saved.
Senegal then triumphed 1-0 after extra time, with Pape Gueye scoring the winner.
That result was overturned almost two months later when a Confederation of African Football (Caf) appeals board decreed the Teranga Lions had breached competition regulations by leaving the field of play after the penalty was awarded.
Senegal's football federation (FSF) subsequently appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), sport's highest legal authority, with a three-man panel hearing its case behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.
In a unanimous verdict, the Cas panel has effectively backed the decision by referee Jean-Jacques Ndala to restart the game after Senegal returned to the field and the match was played to a conclusion. The result of the final stands and Senegal are now confirmed as Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) 2025 winners.
A statement issued by Cas said the court considered that "the referee's decision to resume the match or to stop it fell definitively within his sole authority".
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume."
The FSF immediately reacted with a social media post featuring a picture of the side lifting the trophy in January captioned with the phrase "again and always champions of Africa".
"The FSF welcomes this ruling with deep satisfaction," it later said in a statement.
"This decision affirms, above all, the triumph of sporting fairness and reaffirms a fundamental principle: the true outcome of a match is determined exclusively on the field of play, under the protection of sports law."
Meanwhile, Morocco's football federation (FRMF) expressed "surprise" at the ruling and added that it would "pursue all available legal avenues to challenge the decision".
Caf says it respects the Cas award and "will take all the necessary measures to implement it".
The full grounds for the decision will be published by Cas in due course unless the parties request confidentiality.
'Shameful' and 'terrible look' - the chaos that marred Afcon 2025 final
'The longest VAR check in history' - the fallout from shock Afcon decision
Senegal's walk-off during the final in Rabat has already brought about a change in football's rules.
"The referee may sanction with a red card any player who leaves the field of play in protest at ⁠a ​referee's decision," said Ifab, the game's lawmaking body, in April.
"This new rule will also apply ​to any team official who incites players to leave the field of play. A team that causes a match ​to be abandoned will, in principle, forfeit the match."
Morocco and Senegal have both changed coach since the Afcon 2025 final and earlier this month secured their places at the 2027 edition of the tournament with two rounds of qualification remaining.
Referee Ndala was at the centre of the controversy during the Afcon final
A tightly contested final between the continent's top-ranked sides produced two moments of controversy in second-half stoppage time, with referee Ndala at the centre of the drama.
First the Congolese official denied Senegal a near-certain goal, blowing his whistle for a challenge by Abdoulaye Seck on Morocco right-back Achraf Hakimi moments before Ismaila Sarr nodded in.
The free-kick looked soft, but the video assistant referee (VAR) was unable to get involved because Ndala had awarded the foul before the ball crossed the line.
Three minutes later came a flashpoint in the Senegal box, when El Hadji Malick Diouf tugged Morocco playmaker Diaz back before heading a corner clear.
Diaz vehemently claimed a penalty and Ndala eventually awarded a spot-kick after being sent to consult his pitchside monitor by the VAR.
Senegal coach Pape Thiaw called his players over to the touchline, and Thiaw subsequently headed down the tunnel to the changing room in protest against the decision - accompanied by several players.

Senegal have been confirmed as winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) overturned a ruling that had stripped them of the title and handed it to hosts Morocco.
The court, based in Lausanne, Switzerland, upheld an appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF) against a decision by the Confederation of African Football's (CAF) appeal board. The board had declared that Senegal forfeited the final and recorded Morocco as 3-0 winners. The original 1-0 result in Senegal's favour now stands.
"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the Referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met - both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," the court said.
"In the Panel's view, there is no doubt that the effects of the Referee's decision were limited to the pitch. As such, the Panel considers that the Referee's decision was covered by the 'field of play' doctrine."
Under the doctrine, CAS does not review decisions taken on the pitch by referees unless the rules were applied arbitrarily or in bad faith.
"The Panel acknowledged that the Referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension. However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary'," CAS added.
The Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF) said it would "pursue all necessary legal avenues" to contest the ruling.
The FRMF said it objected to the rejection of its request to postpone the decision. It added that it could take the case to Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court, which rules on procedural matters rather than the merits of a case.
In a statement, the FRMF referred to what it said was "contact" between Ulrich Haas, a German arbitrator who was one of the three CAS panel members, and the president of the FSF 48 hours before the decision was announced.
The final was played on 18 January at the Prince Moulay Abdellah Stadium in Rabat, Morocco. The score was 0-0 deep into stoppage time when the Congolese referee, Jean-Jacques Ngambo Ndala, awarded Morocco a penalty after a VAR review.
Senegal's players, led by coach Pape Thiaw, walked off the pitch in protest for 15 minutes, and fans tried to storm the field.
When play resumed, Brahim Díaz's penalty was saved by Senegal goalkeeper Édouard Mendy. Pape Gueye then scored in extra time to win the match for Senegal.
CAF's disciplinary board first fined and banned players and officials from both Senegal and Morocco, with fines totalling more than $1 million, but it left the result unchanged.
Morocco appealed. In March, CAF's appeal board ruled that Senegal's conduct fell under Articles 82 and 84 of the tournament regulations, declared that they had forfeited the final, and awarded Morocco their first African title since 1976.
The FSF lodged its appeal with CAS on 25 March. Morocco's football federation argued that the referee's decision was not protected by the "field of play" doctrine, that by leaving the pitch Senegal had breached Articles 82 and 84, and that the referee should have ended the match early.
The panel rejected those arguments. It found that the two articles apply only when a team's conduct leads a referee to abandon a match permanently, so they did not apply in this case. A hearing was held behind closed doors in Lausanne on 8 October.
CAS noted that the FSF, Thiaw and some players had already been sanctioned by CAF in separate disciplinary proceedings.

Israeli airstrikes in the Gaza Strip killed seven people on Tuesday, including Hamas's director of internal security, according to Palestinian officials, despite a ceasefire that has been in place since October 2025.
Gaza's interior ministry, which operates under Hamas authority, said an airstrike in Gaza City killed Brigadier General Naeem Abu Nahal, director-general of the Internal Security Service.
Israel's military said it had "struck a senior terrorist" from Hamas.
Mahmoud Bassal, spokesman for Gaza's civil defence agency, said several other people were in critical condition after the same strike in Gaza City's Rimal neighbourhood.
Bassal said three people, including a 17-year-old, had been killed earlier on Tuesday in a separate Israeli airstrike near Gaza City.
Three more were killed in a third strike, on a police station in the Al-Mawasi area of southern Gaza, he added.
Gaza's police force, which also operates under Hamas, said two policemen aged 23 and 33 were among the dead. It condemned the strike as "part of an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus".
Israel's military said it had "struck terrorists in the area" of the police station, but did not confirm the strike that is believed to have killed the 17-year-old.
Israel and Hamas regularly accuse each other of violating the ceasefire, which came into effect after two years of war triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
More than 1,650 Palestinians have been killed since the truce began, according to a tally based on data from Gaza's health ministry, which also operates under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Over the same period, the Israeli military says seven of its soldiers and one civilian contractor have been killed.
Most of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced and living in tents or makeshift shelters. Israel's military says it controls more than 60% of the territory.
The strikes come as talks continue in Israel to form a new government after legislative elections in October produced no clear winner.
The centrist Gadi Eisenkot is seeking to build a coalition that would end the long tenure of Benjamin Netanyahu, who is now caretaker prime minister.
But Netanyahu, who has staked his reputation on ensuring Israel's security since the 7 October attack, remains in charge of military operations while negotiations go on.

A funeral was held earlier in southern Gaza for three Palestinians killed in an Israeli strike
At least seven Palestinians, including a senior Hamas security official, have been killed in Israeli air strikes in the Gaza Strip, health officials and first responders say.
Naeem Abu Nahel, the head of Hamas's internal security service, was targeted in western Gaza City, Gaza's Hamas-run interior ministry said. The 50-year-old had only been in the position since September, when his predecessor was captured in a raid by Israeli special forces .
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz announced that Abu Nahel was "eliminated" by the Israeli military.
The six other people were killed in two earlier air strikes elsewhere in Gaza.
Three people, including a teenage boy, were killed in the Wadi Gaza area, south of Gaza City, according to the health officials and first responders. The other three were killed at a police station in the al-Mawasi area, west of Khan Younis, they added.
Gaza's police force, which operates under the interior ministry, said two of its officers were among those who died in the second attack. It also accused Israel of "an ongoing campaign targeting the police apparatus aimed at sowing chaos" in the territory.
The Israeli military said it struck "military operatives" in both areas.
Witnesses said an Israeli drone targeted Naeem Abu Nahel as he was walking on a side street near a tent camp for displaced people in Gaza City.
Several other people were reportedly seriously injured in the strike.
The Israeli military said Abu Nahel had "possessed extensive institutional knowledge" about Hamas's internal security service - which is responsible for enforcing discipline, protecting infrastructure and rooting out informants - and that his death constituted "a blow to the apparatus's management capabilities".
It also alleged that he had advanced attacks on Israeli troops and civilians during the war and that it killed him "to remove the threat he posed".
Gaza's interior ministry said Abu Nahel's killing followed what it described as the internal security service's "important achievements in combating gangs collaborating with the occupation [Israel] and operating in areas under the control of its military".
Gaza's health ministry warned that there was a rapid rise in cases of meningitis in October
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,679 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to thousands of shelters for displaced families.
The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
On Tuesday, the health ministry warned that there had been a rapid rise in cases of meningitis, with 272 reported in October - about eight times the usual monthly average.
Fifteen deaths had been attributed to the infection so far this year, including five reported between August and October, it said.
Israeli military body Cogat said on Monday it was "working to provide a dedicated humanitarian response" and that a newly approved package of pumps, generators, water tankers and medical equipment had been presented at a meeting with UN agencies.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,740 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

Real Madrid come from behind to power past PSV Eindhoven with a 5-1 win in football’s Champions League.
Jude Bellingham scored a sensational goal to help Real Madrid come from behind to thrash PSV 5-1 in the Champions League on Tuesday, continuing their 100 percent start.
Kylian Mbappe netted a brace with Federico Valverde and Vinicius Junior also on target for Los Blancos, who fought back strongly in the second half after Ivan Perisic sent the visitors ahead from the penalty spot.
Madrid climbed provisionally top of the league phase standings with their fifth victory from five European matches, and 10th consecutive triumph across all football competitions.
PSV put up an impressive fight in the first half, but Jose Mourinho’s side blew them away with a dynamic showing in the second, inspired by England midfielder Bellingham.
The former Birmingham and Borussia Dortmund star watched the first half from the bench, with Mourinho explaining he had a minor fitness issue.
However, with Madrid trailing to Perisic’s penalty, Mourinho called on Bellingham at the interval, and the 23-year-old inspired a memorable second-half display at the Santiago Bernabeu.
Ruben van Bommel drilled wide early on for Dutch champions PSV, while Vinicius crashed a shot off the bar at the other end.
PSV took the lead when Aurelien Tchouameni trod on Sven Mijnans’s foot, and Perisic rifled in the resulting penalty.
Mourinho made a triple change at half-time, including bringing on Bellingham, and Madrid were transformed.
Five minutes into the second half, the record 15-time champions were level, with Valverde finishing a slick team move.
Vinicius, who looked more like himself after a shaky start to the season, crossed for Yan Diomande to feed Arda Guler. The Turkish midfielder’s gentle back-heel flick set up Valverde to drive home at the near post.
Madrid were rampant, and after PSV goalkeeper Matej Kovar saved from Guler and Mbappe, Bellingham netted a marvellous second.
The midfielder collected a loose ball on the edge of the box, flicked it up and then sliced a stunning volley across the despairing Kovar and inside the post.
Vinicius was denied one-on-one before Mbappe netted Madrid’s third with a clinical finish after being set up by Guler.
Mbappe, who has scored in each of Madrid’s Champions League matches this season, rounded the goalkeeper to add a fourth.
Vinicius scored his first goal for Madrid since August to wrap things up after Bellingham lobbed a pass in behind PSV’s battered defence.
Mourinho jumped up in celebration after Vinicius prodded home, with the Portuguese coach hoping it will herald an overdue return to form for the Brazilian international.

Colombian President says Villavicencio bomb attack came in retaliation of government offensives.
Bogota, Colombia – Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has blamed ex-FARC rebels for a car bomb attack last night targeting a state government building, which injured at least 23 people.
On a visit to Villavicencio on Tuesday, where the attack took place, the president accused Antonio Medina, a commander of the Central General Staff (EMC) rebel group, of plotting the bombing in retaliation for government offensives in the province.
“The bandit Antonio Medina from the [FARC] dissidents is to blame, and we’re going to go after him and make him pay with blood,” de la Espriella told reporters.
Last night’s attack rocked the seat of government in Meta, a province bordering the capital, Bogota, to the southeast. Videos show extensive damage to the building in Villavicencio, which houses the governor’s office, as well as surrounding businesses and vehicles.
The Head of National Police Operations, Ricardo Alarcon, told local media that initial tests indicate the car was laden with between 80 and 100kg (176-220 pounds) of pentolite, a high explosive used in military warheads, as well as civilian mining.
Meta was a historical heartland for the FARC, which officially demobilised following a historic peace deal in 2016. In the years since, dissident rebels who refused to lay down their arms or returned to war have expanded their control in the province, a key access point to the coca plantations, gold mining and drug smuggling routes of the Amazon River Basin.
The most powerful group is the EMC, headed by alias Ivan Mordisco, one of Colombia’s most wanted men. The government earlier this year announced a bounty of 5 billion pesos (roughly $1.4m) for his capture or killing.
In recent months, the government has increased pressure on the EMC, bombing its camps and targeting senior members. Just yesterday, the president confirmed the killing of alias El Churco, an EMC commander.
The campaign is part of the new far-right government’s security pivot, which aims to tackle criminal organisations through military force and has suspended the negotiations initiated under the previous government.
De la Espriella has suggested that last night’s bombing in Villavicencio was likely a retaliation against ramped-up state pressure on armed groups.
“The narco-terrorists are running wild, launching desperate attacks, because they know we are defeating them and that their end is near,” the president wrote on X this morning.
The attack, which happened on the eve of the 10-year anniversary of the 2016 peace deal, highlights the growing risks to civilians under de la Espriella’s heavy-handed security strategy, say experts.
“As the government increases pressure, armed and criminal groups are trying to raise the cost of doing that for the government by exerting pain, instilling fear and causing direct harm against communities and against the civilian population,” said Elizabeth Dickinson, deputy director for Latin America at the International Crisis Group.

Manchester City, meanwhile, twice came from behind to draw 2-2 with Napoli, while Arsenal were held to a 1-1 draw by Borussia Dortmund.
The Champions League followed a recent script for two of Europe’s heavyweight teams Tuesday, with Real Madrid — helped by a long-range stunner from Jude Bellingham and Kylian Mbappé 's double — recovering to beat PSV Eindhoven 5-1 for a fifth straight victory in the league phase and City’s underwhelming form continuing with a 2-2 draw against Napoli in Kevin De Bruyne's latest homecoming.
Arsenal was held to a 1-1 draw by Borussia Dortmund and Como won again to move into third place after five rounds of games.
Slovan Bratislava, meanwhile, remained the only team on zero points after a 15th straight loss in the competition's main phase — this time 2-0 to Real Betis.
Make that 10 straight wins in all competitions for Madrid, whose resurgence under Jose Mourinho will be a concern for the rest of European soccer.
Things weren't going so well against PSV on Tuesday after a 32nd-minute penalty by Ivan Perisic for the Dutch league leaders.
Enter Bellingham, who had started on the bench and was introduced at halftime to revitalize Madrid’s attack at the Santiago Bernabeu Stadium.
After Federico Valverde equalized, Bellingham scored one of the best goals of this season's competition by teeing the ball up with the left foot, then with his right foot, before sending a looping volley with the outside of his right foot in off the post.
Mbappé added to the lead with goals in the 64th and 84th minutes, maintaining his record of scoring in every Champions League game so far this campaign, and Vinícius Júnior grabbed a fifth in the 87th.
Madrid, which previously had winners in the 90th minute or later against Roma and AEK Athens, has 15 points — three more than Paris Saint-Germain, which hosts Roma on Wednesday.
City's winless streak in Premier League reached four matches at the weekend, and there was no respite in the Champions League.
Rayan Cherki did at least rescue a point after City twice went behind to Napoli, for whom De Bruyne — a City great — started and was applauded off the field when substituted in the second half.
City looked in danger of falling to a second defeat in this season’s competition after Noa Lang’s volley put Napoli 2-1 ahead at Etihad Stadium.
Enzo Maresca’s team had already fought back from 1-0 down, with Ayyoub Bouaddi leveling after Rasmus Hojlund’s opener.
Cherki wriggled into the box and fired low inside the near post in the 86th
In a clash of the English and German league leaders, Arsenal and Dortmund both scored high-quality goals.
Viktor Gyökeres sent a dipping shot up and over Dortmund’s tall goalkeeper Gregor Kobel in the 10th, before Maximilian Beier leveled in the 55th with a slick low shot past Kepa Arrizabalaga. That was created by a surging run from teenage French defender Joane Gadou.
Arsenal remains unbeaten for two full years in the Champions League main phase and next hosts table-topping Real Madrid in two weeks’ time.
Como's debut campaign in the Champions League could hardly be going better.
There were none of the fireworks that marked the record 9-1 rout of Lens in the last round, but beating AEK 1-0 through Luis Milla’s rising strike means Cesc Fabregas’s team is surely heading into the knockout rounds
Como has 12 points and another win, maybe against Real Betis next, could even wind up securing a top-eight finish and automatic qualification to the last 16. After that, Como must play Barcelona and PSG .
Bodø/Glimt and Galatasaray both left it late to earn scrappy 1-0 wins over LASK and Aston Villa, respectively, in the early kickoffs.
A humble club from a fishing town of around 55,000 people in northern Norway, Bodø/Glimt is making another run for the knockout stage — a year after providing one of the storylines of last season’s competition by advancing to the last 16, beating Man City, Atletico Madrid and Inter Milan along the way.
The team now has two wins from five matches and is on seven points after Andreas Helmersen’s back-post header deflected in off LASK substitute Melayro Bogarde in the second minute of stoppage time.
Villa was back in Istanbul for the first time since winning the Europa League there in May, beating Freiburg 3-0 in the final.
It wasn't an enjoyable return. The English club didn’t even have a shot on target against Galatasaray, with Deniz Gül scoring the only goal with a close-range header.
Feyenoord and Porto drew 0-0 and Lens lost a fourth game out of five, 3-1 at Leipzig.
